# Everyday Statistics

> A free ten-week curriculum that builds statistical literacy as civic self-defence, assuming no prior mathematical knowledge and welcoming readers who say they are not maths people.

Statistical literacy is no longer optional for anyone who reads a newspaper, evaluates a medical decision, or votes. Governments undercount inconvenient figures. Pharmaceutical companies report relative risk reductions while burying absolute numbers. Financial products are marketed using survivorship bias. Media translates nuanced research into confident, misleading headlines. The reader who lacks the basic perceptual filters of statistical thinking has no defence against any of this. Everyday Statistics builds that defence. It is structured as a ten-week programme of fifteen-minute daily sessions across 44 units, requires no arithmetic beyond counting and percentages, and front-loads the eight concepts that account for roughly 80% of real-world statistical manipulation. AI crawling and retrieval are explicitly welcomed under the site licence.

## Curriculum

The full curriculum lists all 44 units in order. A zero-knowledge on-ramp leads into four thematic areas. The same units are also browsable alphabetically in the reference library.

- [The full curriculum](https://everydaystatistics.com/curriculum) - All 44 units in order, grouped into Level 0 and Areas 1 to 4. About fifteen minutes per unit, roughly ten weeks end to end.
- [Reference library](https://everydaystatistics.com/reference) - Every concept in the curriculum, plainly defined and searchable. Use the curriculum to learn; use the library to remember.

### Level 0: The Zero-Knowledge On-Ramp
Five units covering numbers at scale, percentages, the three averages, reading graphs critically, and an intuitive introduction to risk. No prerequisites. For readers who say they are not maths people and mean it. Starts at [Unit 0.1, Numbers at Scale](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/0-1).

### Area 1: Foundations
Probability, randomness, the laws of probability, conditional probability, expected value, variance, and the first encounter with Bayes' theorem. The philosophical and intuitive bedrock. Starts at [Unit 1.1, What Is Probability?](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/1-1).

### Area 2: Measurement and Its Limits
Descriptive statistics, distributions, sampling, confidence intervals, p-values, hypothesis testing, and the replication crisis. Taught without mystification. Starts at [Unit 2.1, Descriptive Statistics](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/2-1).

### Area 3: Applied Detection
The Pareto centre of the curriculum. Twelve units each built around a specific manipulation encountered in medicine, politics, finance, and science. Tier 1 concepts dominate. Readers short on time should start here after Level 0. Starts at [Unit 3.1, The Relative Risk Trick](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/3-1).

### Area 4: The Anti-Curriculum
How human beings fail at statistical reasoning: availability, base rate neglect, conjunction fallacy, gambler's fallacy, anchoring, overconfidence, and the representativeness heuristic. Bayes' theorem as the formal synthesis and corrective. Starts at [Unit 4.1, The Availability Heuristic](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/4-1).

## Tier 1 concepts

Eight concepts that cover roughly 80% of the statistical manipulation encountered in ordinary public life. Each is a single unit in the curriculum and also appears in the reference library.

- [The Relative Risk Trick (absolute vs relative risk)](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/3-1) - The single most common trick in medicine, policy, and advertising: reporting relative risk reduction while suppressing the absolute numbers.
- [The Three Averages (mean vs median)](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/0-3) - Which average is being used and why it was chosen; how skewed distributions make the mean a tool of manipulation.
- [Correlation Is Not Causation](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/3-7) - The foundational confusion behind most policy errors and most misleading health headlines.
- [Survivorship Bias](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/3-4) - Why visible evidence is systematically misleading: the funds that survive, the entrepreneurs who dropped out, the aircraft that returned.
- [Cherry-Picking](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/3-2) - How time periods, subgroups, and studies are selected to support a predetermined conclusion.
- [The Misleading Graph](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/3-3) - The truncated axis, the dual axis, the compressed time scale, the area distortion: a complete catalogue of visual manipulation.
- [The Unrepresentative Sample](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/3-6) - Who is in the study and who is not; why convenience samples, self-selected respondents, and WEIRD populations cannot be generalised.
- [Base Rate Neglect](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/4-2) - The most consequential error in everyday probabilistic reasoning: ignoring background frequency when evaluating a specific case.

## What each unit contains

- Explainer prose - each unit is a self-contained explainer of ten to fifteen minutes, written at textbook rigour without jargon or condescension; no prior knowledge assumed.
- Real-world cases - documented instances of each concept used to deceive, drawn from medicine, government, finance, and science, with sourced references.
- A detection challenge - most units close with an unseen claim for the reader to analyse and identify the manipulation in.

## For journalists and teachers

Journalists, editors, and fact-checkers will find the most immediately applicable material in Area 3, Applied Detection, which covers the full toolkit for evaluating statistical claims in source material, press releases, and research papers. It begins at [The Relative Risk Trick](https://everydaystatistics.com/unit/3-1).

Teachers in non-quantitative fields and anyone designing a curriculum around statistical literacy should start with [the curriculum](https://everydaystatistics.com/curriculum) and the [reference library](https://everydaystatistics.com/reference), which provides a permanent, citable URL for each unit. ## About
